families.name: Ruy Lopez
families.idea: Pressure the knight that defends e5, then the long manoeuvring game with c3 and d4.
masters: Named after the Spanish priest Ruy López de Segura, who wrote about it in 1561.
Fischer made the Exchange Variation (4.Bxc6) a serious weapon in the 1960s.

families.name: Scotch Game
families.idea: Open the centre at once with d4 and play against Black's pieces rather than a slow manoeuvring game.
masters: Kasparov brought it back to the top level, including in his 1990 match against Karpov.

families.name: Vienna Game
families.idea: Nc3 first, then the f4 break: a King's Gambit idea with more preparation.

families.name: King's Gambit
families.idea: Sacrifice the f-pawn for fast development and an open f-file against Black's king.
masters: The signature opening of the Romantic era; Spassky beat Fischer with it at Mar del Plata in 1960.

families.name: Caro-Kann Defence
families.idea: Prepare ...d5 with ...c6 so your light-squared bishop gets out before ...e6: solid, with few weaknesses.
masters: Named after Horatio Caro and Marcus Kann, who analysed it in the 1880s.

families.name: French Defence
families.idea: ...e6 and ...d5: a solid chain, counterplay with ...c5 and ...f6 against White's centre.
masters: Botvinnik's main defence; the Winawer was his weapon in world championship play.

families.name: Scandinavian Defence
families.idea: Hit e4 on move one and develop the queen early, with a simple, sound structure.
masters: Anand used it as Black against Kasparov in their 1995 world championship match.

families.name: Pirc Defence
families.idea: Let White build a centre, then fianchetto and strike at it with ...c6, ...e5 or ...c5.

ruy-exch.name: Ruy Lopez: Exchange Variation
ruy-exch.idea: Trade the bishop for the knight to double Black's c-pawns, then aim for an endgame where your healthy kingside majority counts.
notes: Centre pawn plus open lines.
Black claims the centre.
Attack e5.
Defend e5.
The Spanish bishop hits the defender of e5.
The Morphy Defence: put the question to the bishop.
The Exchange Variation: give up the bishop pair to damage Black's pawns.
Recapturing toward the centre opens Black's queen and c8-bishop; the doubled c-pawns are the long-term cost.
Castle. Now Nxe5 is a real threat, because the c6-knight is gone.
Black props up e5 with the f-pawn, a main line.
Open the centre while you are better developed.
Black gives up the centre pawn.
The knight lands in the centre.
Kick the knight away from d4.
Retreat; from b3 the knight eyes c5 and a5.
Black trades queens. In the endgame your four kingside pawns against three are the asset.
Recapture onto the open d-file. Plan: Be3, Nc3, f3 and later push the kingside majority.

why: ...c6 supports ...d5 without blocking the c8-bishop, which is the French's problem with ...e6.
Trade in the centre; White's knight recaptures.
The bishop develops outside the pawn chain and hits the knight.
Keep the bishop: it is Black's best piece in the Caro-Kann.
White threatens h5, chasing the bishop.
Give the bishop a retreat on h7 before h5 arrives.
White gains kingside space and fixes your g-pawn. That h5 pawn can become a target later.
Trade your bishop for White's best attacking piece.
Now ...e6 costs nothing: the bishop is already gone, so nothing is shut in. Plans: ...Ngf6, ...Qc7, often long castling, and ...c5 later.

carokann-adv.name: Caro-Kann: Advance Variation
carokann-adv.idea: Get the light-squared bishop out to f5 before ...e6, then hit White's pawn chain at its base with ...c5.
notes: White takes the centre.
The Caro-Kann: prepare ...d5 while keeping the c8-bishop's diagonal open.
White builds the full centre.
Challenge e4 straight away.
The Advance: White grabs space and takes f6 away from your knight.
The point of the Caro-Kann: develop the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6.
White develops calmly (the Short System).
Now ...e6 completes a solid chain behind the bishop.
White prepares to castle.
Hit the base of White's chain: ...c5 is your main lever in Advance structures.
White adds a defender to d4.
Release the tension; White must recapture with a piece.
White's knight takes the central square.
The knight heads for c6 (or g6), then the f8-bishop develops. Plan: ...Nbc6 or ...Nec6, ...a6, and pressure on e5.

carokann-exch.name: Caro-Kann: Exchange Variation
carokann-exch.idea: A Queen's Gambit structure with colours reversed: develop actively, then use the half-open c-file and the minority attack ...b5-b4.
notes: White takes the centre.
Prepare ...d5.
White builds the centre.
Challenge e4.
The Exchange: White releases the tension.
Recapture with the c-pawn: you get the half-open c-file and keep a pawn on d5.
The bishop aims at h7 and stops ...Bf5 for now.
Develop and pressure d4.
White supports d4: the Carlsbad structure, colours reversed.
Develop toward the kingside.
White's dark-squared bishop takes the active diagonal.
Develop the bishop with tempo on the queen, before ...e6 shuts it in. White usually answers Qb3, hitting b7 and d5. Plan: ...e6, ...Bd6, then ...b5-b4.

french-exch.name: French Defence: Exchange Variation
french-exch.idea: Symmetrical pawns, so active pieces decide: your c8-bishop is free, so develop fast and copy nothing blindly.
notes: White takes the centre.
The French: prepare ...d5 with a pawn behind it.
White builds the centre.
Challenge e4.
The Exchange: White gives up the space fight for a symmetrical game.
Recapture. Your c8-bishop is free now, the French's usual problem piece.
White develops.
Active development on the best diagonal.
White mirrors.
From e7 the knight leaves the f-pawn free and can go to f5 or g6.
White castles.
Castle. Next: ...Bf5 or ...Bg4 and ...Nbc6, with full equality.

why: Hit e4 on move one, before White can support it.
The queen comes out early. Normally that costs time, but here White gains only one tempo, with Nc3.
On a5 the queen is safe from attacks, and once White plays d4 it pins the c3-knight to the king.
Bishop out before ...e6, the same idea as the Caro-Kann.
...e6 and next ...c6 make your position very hard to break.
White breaks the pin and sets a trap: if the c3-knight jumps, the d2-bishop attacks your queen.
...c6 gives the queen a retreat on c7 and takes b5 and d5 from White's knight.
